title: Rivers of living water (John 7:37–39)
hook: on the feast's last day he stands and cries out

segments.voice: Yesterday, Capernaum emptying out, and Peter staying anyway. Your line was words of eternal life.

Autumn in Jerusalem, and the city is full of huts. For the feast of Tabernacles, families build shelters of branches on rooftops and in courtyards and live in them for a week, remembering the years in the desert. It's a harvest festival, and a prayer for rain before the dry ground has to be planted. Each morning of the feast, according to the old Jewish sources, a priest carried water up from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it out at the altar, with trumpets and singing. On the last day, the great day, Jesus stands up and shouts.
screen: `A CITY FULL OF HUTS.` → `WATER POURED AT THE ALTAR.` → `ON THE LAST DAY, HE SHOUTS.`

segments.voice: John says he stood and cried out, a man on his feet, raising his voice over a festival crowd. In the Douay-Rheims: "If any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink." Then: "He that believeth in me, as the scripture saith, Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Out of his belly sounds strange in English. The Greek word means the belly, the inside, the deepest part of a person; we'd say the heart, or the gut. We've heard living water before, at the well in Samaria. Here it isn't a cup. It's rivers. And John stops to tell us what it means: this he said of the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive; the Spirit wasn't yet given, because Jesus wasn't yet glorified. So the water poured at the altar becomes a picture of something still to come. Here's an old puzzle: the sentence can be divided two ways. The Douay reads it as the believer's belly. But some early Christian writers read it as Christ's own: let the one who believes come and drink, for out of him flow rivers. Both readings have histories in the Church, and some readers hear them together: the Spirit flows from Christ, and then through the believer to others. John may be pointing ahead, too. At the cross, a soldier's spear opens Jesus's side, and blood and water come out. The Catechism sees the sacraments, and the Church itself, flowing from that wound.
screen: `THE FEAST OF TABERNACLES.` · `IF ANY MAN THIRST, COME.` · `OUT OF HIS BELLY: WHOSE?` · `THIS HE SAID OF THE SPIRIT.` · then, large: `RIVERS OF LIVING WATER.`

segments.voice: Breathe in and notice something you've been given lately, a kindness, rest, an idea, time; breathe out slowly and picture some of it flowing on, past you, to someone else, because a river doesn't keep its water. If you pray, ask that what you've been given flow out; if not, just let one person come to mind who could use it.
Rivers of living water. Jesus's cry on the last day of Tabernacles; John says he meant the Spirit, flowing out of the one who believes. Today's word.
Your line: out of his belly. Not a cup of water, but rivers. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 506 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

howItsDone: Catholics hear John 7:37–39 at the Vigil Mass of Pentecost, linking the rivers of living water to the gift of the Holy Spirit.

chat.says: In John 7, what are the "rivers of living water" Jesus shouts about at the feast?
options: John tells us: the Spirit, given to those who believe once Jesus was glorified.
The water poured at the altar, which he promised would never run dry again.
The Jordan River, where he told the crowd to go and be baptized by John.
chat.meaning: John adds his own note: this he said of the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive.

Tabernacles.meaning: the autumn feast when families live a week in huts

Siloam.meaning: the pool where water was drawn for the altar

Samaria.meaning: the region of the well where living water was first offered

Catechism.meaning: the Catholic Church's summary of its teaching

notes: Water-drawing rite at Tabernacles from Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 (golden flagon from Siloam, poured at the altar); 'trumpets and singing' from the surrounding passages. Confirm details and that 'each morning' fits (the Mishnah describes it on the seven days).
Two punctuations of John 7:37–38 (believer vs Christ as source) presented without ranking. Confirm.
Link to John 19:34 and the sacraments flowing from Christ's side (cf. CCC 1225, Sacrosanctum Concilium 5). Confirm.
Lectionary: John 7:37–39 at the Pentecost Vigil. Confirm.
'Teachers usually sat' (cf. Luke 4:20; Matthew 5:1) is a general observation; confirm or soften.
